source.title: *Harlow v. Brightwater Logistics, Inc.*, No. 27-CV-24-0117 (Minn. Dist. Ct. 2025) (synthetic)
source.text: To prevail on a breach-of-contract claim, a plaintiff must prove (1) the formation of a contract, (2) the plaintiff's performance of any conditions precedent, and (3) the defendant's breach. A plaintiff must prove damages to recover more than nominal damages, but nominal damages remain available for any proven breach. Summary judgment is appropriate only when no genuine dispute of material fact exists and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. A written contract that bars oral modification ordinarily controls, except where the party seeking enforcement has waived the bar by its own conduct. Here, Brightwater accepted late deliveries for eight months without objection, so a jury could find waiver. The motion is DENIED.

source.title: Defendant's Memorandum in Support of Motion to Dismiss, *Osterberg Outdoor Supply Co. v. Quillfeather Ceramics GmbH*, No. 25-cv-2290 (D. Minn.) (synthetic)
source.text: Plaintiff bears the burden of making a prima facie showing of personal jurisdiction over each defendant. Quillfeather has no office, employees, or bank accounts in Minnesota, and it shipped no product here; a distributor resold the mugs without Quillfeather's direction. The mere foreseeability that a product may reach the forum state does not establish purposeful availment. *Ostrander v. Pell Manufacturing Co.*, No. 22-cv-0940 (D. Minn. 2023). Quillfeather supports this motion with a sworn declaration, which shifts the burden to Plaintiff to come forward with evidence, not allegations.

source.title: *Trial Practice Field Guide*, ch. 7, "Expert Witnesses" (Lindqvist & Ober LLP internal know-how, 2025) (synthetic)
source.text: On direct, ask open-ended questions and let your expert teach; jurors trust the witness, not the lawyer. The rules of evidence generally prohibit leading questions on direct but permit them on cross. At the opposing expert's deposition, lock in every opinion she plans to offer and every document she relied on. Do not argue with the expert at deposition; you will only educate her for trial. Close each topic by asking, "Have you now told me all the bases for that opinion?"

source.title: *Reliance Without a Bargain: Promissory Estoppel and the Mid-Employment Noncompete*, 41 Northland L. Rev. 233 (2025) (synthetic)
source.text: Courts increasingly decline to enforce a noncompete agreement that an employee signed after starting work unless the employer supplied fresh consideration. A raise, a promotion, or access to new confidential information can serve; continued at-will employment often cannot. When the agreement fails for want of consideration, some employers turn to promissory estoppel, but that doctrine protects reliance on a promise, not an employer's expectation of restraint. This Article argues that courts should reject the estoppel route outright.

source.title: Northland Consumer Data Breach Notification Act, Nland. Stat. § 325X.04 (2025) (synthetic)
source.text: (a) A business that discovers a data breach shall notify each affected resident within 45 days after discovery. (b) The notice must describe the categories of personal information involved and the steps the resident can take to protect against identity theft. (c) A business may delay notice at the written request of a law enforcement agency, and a delay so requested does not violate subdivision (a). (d) A business that fails to give timely notice is subject to a civil penalty of up to $500 for each affected resident. (e) An affected resident may bring a civil action for damages caused by a violation of this section. (f) A business may not require a resident to waive any right under this section, and any such waiver is void. (g) An action under this section must be commenced within two years after the resident receives notice.

source.title: Northland Civil Jury Instruction Guide, CIVJIG 25.10, "Negligence: Definition and Direct Cause" (synthetic)
source.text: Every person has a duty to use reasonable care to avoid harming others. Negligence is the failure to use reasonable care. Reasonable care is the care a reasonable person would use in the same or similar circumstances. The plaintiff must prove by the greater weight of the evidence that the defendant was negligent and that the negligence was a direct cause of the harm. A direct cause is a cause that had a substantial part in bringing about the harm.

source.title: *Vendor SaaS Agreement Negotiation Playbook*, § 4, "Liability" (Fernhollow Analytics in-house legal team, 2025) (synthetic)
source.text: Never accept a limitation of liability clause that caps the vendor's exposure below twelve months of fees. Carve out data breaches, confidentiality breaches, and indemnification obligations from the cap. Require the vendor to notify us of any security incident within 72 hours. A force majeure clause should not excuse the vendor's obligation to maintain backups and restore service. Push back on any late-payment penalty above 1% per month; a court may refuse to enforce a liquidated damages clause that operates as a penalty.

source.title: "Organizational Depositions in Practice," Northland CLE Litigation Institute, session outline, part II (synthetic)
source.text: The noticing party must describe each topic with reasonable particularity; vague topics invite a designee who knows nothing. The organization has a duty to prepare its designee to testify about information reasonably available to it. Serve the deposition notice at least 30 days before the deposition so the organization can prepare. The designee testifies for the organization, so an "I don't know" can bind it at trial. Meet and confer on the topics before the deposition, and confirm the agreed scope in writing.
